note.en: What you see: FAST is a fixed order sweep of four windows in a trauma patient: right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis and subxiphoid heart. Each window asks one question: is there new free fluid or pericardial blood. A positive window shows a dark anechoic stripe where organs should touch. A complete negative set lowers the chance of major bleeding but never rules it out, so the protocol repeats when the patient stays unstable.

steps.en: What you see: FAST is a fixed order sweep of four windows in a trauma patient: right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis and subxiphoid heart. Each window asks one question: is there new free fluid or pericardial blood. A positive window shows a dark anechoic stripe where organs should touch. A complete negative set lowers the chance of major bleeding but never rules it out, so the protocol repeats when the patient stays unstable.
Landmarks to confirm: Morison pouch on the right, splenorenal recess on the left, pelvic pouches behind the bladder, pericardial space around the heart.

Common mistakes and correction: Stopping after one positive window: complete all four since management needs the full map. Calling an empty bladder pelvis negative: fill and repeat. Skipping the left upper quadrant because the right looks clear: the left side is the most commonly missed window.

Normal values with units: No numeric threshold applies. A complete FAST is negative only when all four windows show no new free fluid and no pericardial blood. Any single positive window makes the protocol positive and triggers urgent surgical review.

Pitfalls: Early bleeding may be too small to see on the first pass, so a single negative set never discharges an unstable patient. Clotted blood can look bright and hide among bowel echoes, so correlate with vitals and haemoglobin trend. In pregnancy add the obstetric assessment per local protocol rather than relying on FAST alone.

todo.en: How to get it step by step: Run the windows in the same order every time: right upper quadrant first, then left upper quadrant, then pelvis in two planes, then subxiphoid heart. Spend enough time on each to fan fully, with the left upper quadrant and pelvis each in transverse and lengthwise planes. Call each window positive or negative out loud as it is completed. Repeat the full set when vitals change or the patient remains unstable.

q.en: What is the fixed FAST order?

o.en: Right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis, subxiphoid heart

why.en: The protocol runs right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis, then subxiphoid heart every time.

q.en: One window is positive. What next?

o.en: One positive window is enough to stop
Two planes per window are a waste
Complete all four windows even after a positive one

why.en: Management needs the full map, so complete all four windows.

q.en: When is a FAST set negative?

o.en: All four windows show no new fluid or pericardial blood

why.en: Negative needs all four windows clear of new fluid and pericardial blood.
